 Expansion should not be mistaken for a substitute for separate backup
 In-Depth Review
 The DS1825+ is the archive-first recommendation for photographers whose annual production has outgrown four or five bays. Eight bays let a buyer design around dual parity while retaining useful capacity, mix drive sizes only where the chosen RAID mode permits it, and keep expansion room rather than filling every slot on day one. That matters for wedding studios, schools, agencies, and long-running fine-art projects where the cost of migration is measured in days as well as dollars.
 DSM is a major advantage at this scale. Storage pools, Btrfs snapshots, client backups, remote replication, permissions, and health notifications remain accessible to a photography business without a dedicated administrator. The PCIe slot distinguishes the DS1825+ from compact models: a compatible 10GbE or 25GbE card can prevent the built-in dual 2.5GbE ports from becoming the permanent ceiling. Actual transfer behavior will still depend on the array, clients, switch, and workload; a folder of small Capture One sidecars behaves differently from a 200GB video file.
 An eight-bay tower belongs in a considered physical environment. Eight HDDs, fans, and the power supply produce more noise and vibration than a compact NAS, so a ventilated equipment space is preferable to the edit desk. Use a UPS, monitor temperatures, keep a tested spare-drive procedure, and plan the off-site copy before the volume is full. Expansion to 18 drives is available, but one larger failure domain is not the same as another backup. The DS1825+ is overkill for a hobby library, yet it is a rational long-term base for a professional archive that needs capacity, understandable software, and faster networking on demand.
 Best For
 High-volume studios retaining many years of RAW files
 Teams that need eight-bay RAID flexibility with familiar DSM administration
 Synology DiskStation DS1825+ at B&H , Adorama .
 7. TerraMaster F4-424 Pro 
 Best Compute Value
 Specifications
 Four SATA bays and two M.2 2280 NVMe slots
 Intel Core i3-N305, eight cores; up to 3.8GHz
 32GB DDR5 memory installed
 Two 2.5GbE network ports with link aggregation
 10Gbps USB-C, 10Gbps USB-A, and HDMI 2.1
 Pros
 Powerful CPU and unusually large installed memory for its class
 Compact chassis with dual NVMe support
 Good fit for indexing, containers, and concurrent background jobs
 Competitive diskless cost relative to compute specification
 Cons
 No verified exact Adorama page was found for this article
 No built-in or clearly supported 10GbE path in the selected configuration
 TOS requires more buyer evaluation than the most established NAS platforms
 Four-bay capacity and parity trade-offs remain
 In-Depth Review
 The F4-424 Pro puts its budget into compute and memory. Its Core i3-N305 and 32GB of DDR5 are generous for a four-bay appliance, making it attractive when the NAS will index a large library, generate thumbnails, run containers, and perform backup jobs while serving files. Photographers experimenting with self-hosted gallery, asset-management, or automation services gain far more headroom than a basic ARM or low-memory enclosure provides.
 Storage and network design still set the practical ceiling. Dual 2.5GbE can serve multiple clients or provide failover, but it is not the same as a built-in 10GbE connection for one workstation. Link aggregation usually distributes sessions rather than combining both ports for every transfer. The two M.2 slots can improve supported cache or flash-pool workflows, though the benefit depends on whether the workload is repeated random access, small files, or simple sequential archiving. Four SATA bays make RAID 5 the capacity-oriented choice many buyers will consider, while RAID 6 halves nominal drive count for usable data; neither removes the need for another copy.
 TerraMaster’s TOS has advanced substantially, but this purchase suits someone willing to validate applications, update behavior, restore procedures, and remote-access exposure before trusting a client archive. The stronger processor does not by itself make file protection better. Use snapshots against accidental change, a UPS against abrupt shutdown, and a disconnected or off-site backup against theft, fire, ransomware, and enclosure failure. Choose the F4-424 Pro when background services and memory-heavy tasks matter more than 10GbE. If direct shared video editing is the primary goal, the UGREEN or ASUSTOR alternatives provide faster networking out of the box.
 Best For
 Power users running photo indexing, containers, and several services
 Photographers who prioritize CPU and memory over native 10GbE
 Buy TerraMaster F4-424 Pro from B&H .
 8. QNAP TS-855X 
 Best for Multi-User 10GbE Growth
 Specifications
 Six 3.5-inch SATA bays plus two dedicated 2.5-inch SATA bays
 Two M.2 2280 PCIe Gen3 x4 slots
 Intel Atom C5125, eight cores at 2.8GHz
 8GB DDR4 installed; four slots, 128GB maximum, ECC support
 One 10GBASE-T port, two 2.5GbE ports, and two PCIe Gen3 slots
 Pros
 Built-in 10GbE and dual 2.5GbE support several workstation tiers
 Dedicated SSD bays and M.2 slots enable flexible hybrid storage
 Very high memory ceiling and two PCIe expansion slots
 QNAP states long-term model availability through 2030
 Cons
 Large, heavy, and more infrastructure-oriented than most solo photographers need
 Only six bays accept 3.5-inch HDDs despite the eight-bay name
 8GB base memory may be modest for ambitious QuTS hero configurations
 Administration and security require deliberate attention
 In-Depth Review
 The TS-855X is the long-horizon team option. QNAP combines six full-size HDD bays with two dedicated 2.5-inch SSD bays, two M.2 slots, built-in 10GbE, dual 2.5GbE, and two PCIe slots. That hybrid layout lets a studio keep a high-capacity protected archive on HDDs while assigning SSDs to applications, cache, or a faster working tier under a supported QTS or QuTS hero design. QNAP’s stated long-term availability through 2030 also matters when an organization wants consistent hardware across several locations.
 For photographers, the built-in 10GbE port is the practical centerpiece. One editing workstation can receive a fast path while other staff use 2.5GbE, or the system can attach to a 10GbE switch for shared access. Six HDDs are enough to make dual-parity storage reasonable, but buyers must notice that the remaining two SATA bays are 2.5-inch only. Calling it an eight-bay unit without reading that distinction can produce the wrong capacity plan. The Atom C5125 favors concurrent storage and infrastructure tasks over media-transcoding glamour, while four memory slots and ECC support provide room for growth.
 This is not a plug-in desktop accessory. A secure deployment needs current firmware, minimal exposed services, strong accounts and multifactor authentication where available, snapshot and replication schedules, network segmentation when appropriate, and tested recovery. QuTS hero’s ZFS features also benefit from adequate RAM, so the base 8GB should be evaluated against the selected workload. The TS-855X makes sense for a studio serving several people, maintaining replicated locations, or expecting years of infrastructure growth. A solo photographer wanting quiet simplicity will get more value from the DS1525+ or DS925+.
 Best For
 Multi-user studios standardizing on 10GbE and hybrid storage
 Organizations needing long-term availability, expansion cards, and high memory capacity

 How to Choose a NAS for Photography 
 Start With Usable Capacity, Not Drive Labels
 Add the size of the current archive, annual capture volume, video growth, previews, exports, and a realistic snapshot allowance. Then calculate usable capacity for the chosen RAID level rather than multiplying the number on the drive box by the bay count. Parity, filesystem overhead, reserved free space, and snapshots all reduce what remains. A sensible purchase leaves enough empty space that the next large assignment does not trigger an emergency migration.
 Bay count changes the economics. Four bays are compact, but dual parity consumes half the nominal drives. Five or six bays make stronger redundancy less punitive, and eight bays can accommodate a large archive with room for growth. Larger arrays also add noise, power use, rebuild time, and more components that require monitoring. Prefer CMR NAS or enterprise drives listed as compatible with the exact enclosure, and avoid mixing unverified models merely because their capacities match.
 Match Network Speed to the Actual Edit
 Gigabit Ethernet is adequate for backups and modest browsing, but it becomes conspicuous during large RAW ingests. A 2.5GbE link is a strong baseline for stills and can be deployed over suitable existing Cat 5e cabling. Ten-gigabit networking is more appropriate for several editors, high-resolution video, large panoramas, or frequent transfers measured in hundreds of gigabytes. The enclosure port is only one link: the workstation adapter, switch, cable, RAID, and destination storage must all keep pace.
 Do not assume that bonding two ports doubles a single computer’s transfer rate. Traditional link aggregation usually distributes different sessions or clients. SMB multichannel can use multiple paths in supported configurations, but both ends and the operating system must be configured correctly. One workstation may be served more predictably by a direct 10GbE connection while the NAS uses another port for the ordinary network.
 Separate Originals, Catalogs, Cache, and Backup
 A clean workflow assigns each kind of data an intentional home. Camera originals and finished masters are natural NAS residents. Catalog databases, preview stores, cache, and scratch files may perform better locally and may be unsupported on a network volume; follow the editing application’s current guidance. Fast SSDs can hold active media or supported cache, but cache accelerates access—it does not protect the source files.
 Build the Backup Around Failure Scenarios
 Snapshots help reverse accidental edits and deletions, and RAID can keep work moving after a compatible drive failure. Neither handles every threat. A robust plan keeps at least three copies, on two kinds of storage, with one copy off-site. That may mean the NAS, a rotated external drive, and encrypted cloud or a second NAS at another location. Protect the system with a UPS, enable health notifications, restrict internet exposure, use multifactor authentication where available, and perform test restores before a client deadline proves whether the plan works.
 Conclusion 
 The Synology DS1525+ is the best NAS for most photographers in 2026 because its fifth bay, mature DSM software, ECC memory, optional 10GbE, and expansion path solve more real workflow problems than a narrowly faster specification. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the better value when built-in 10GbE matters and the owner is comfortable validating a younger software platform. For a demanding multi-user studio, the QNAP TVS-h674 provides the compute, six-bay flexibility, ZFS-based QuTS hero tools, and PCIe expansion that a managed creative storage service deserves.
 Whichever enclosure you choose, buy the system rather than the box: compatible drives, enough usable capacity, the right network, a UPS, snapshots, and an independent off-site copy. That complete design—not a RAID badge or peak throughput claim—is what keeps a photo archive accessible and recoverable.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 How many NAS bays does a photographer need?
 Four bays are a practical minimum for many professionals because they permit RAID 5, RAID 6, or RAID 10 choices, but five or six bays make capacity and dual-parity planning less restrictive. High-volume studios may prefer eight bays to leave room for growth without an early migration.
 Is 2.5GbE fast enough for photo editing?
 For one photographer working mainly with RAW stills, 2.5GbE can be a good balance and is much faster than Gigabit Ethernet. Large panoramas, layered PSB files, simultaneous users, and direct video editing benefit more from 10GbE, provided the array, client, switch, and cabling can sustain it.
 Can I put a Lightroom Classic catalog on a NAS?
 Adobe’s normal guidance is to keep the Lightroom Classic catalog on a local drive; originals can live on network storage. Other applications have their own database and collaboration rules, so verify support before moving catalogs, sessions, caches, or libraries to a shared volume.
 Does RAID count as a backup?
 No. RAID can keep a system available after certain drive failures, but it does not protect against accidental deletion, theft, fire, malware, enclosure failure, or every multi-drive event. Maintain an independent local or off-site copy and test restoration.
 Should photographers use HDDs or SSDs in a NAS?
 HDDs provide economical archive capacity; SSDs offer lower latency, quieter operation, and faster working storage at higher cost. A common design uses protected HDDs for originals plus NVMe or SATA SSDs for supported cache or active-project roles, with all important data backed up elsewhere.
 Do I need a UPS for a photo NAS?
 A compatible UPS is strongly recommended. It gives the NAS time to shut down cleanly during an outage and reduces corruption risk, but it is not a surge-proof backup or a substitute for additional data copies.

 Photo storage grows steadily and is difficult to recreate. A useful photo NAS needs enough protected capacity for originals, thumbnails, edits, and several years of growth, plus a separate backup of the irreplaceable files.

 Questions to answer first
 1 How quickly does the original library grow each year? 
 2 Will the NAS index faces, objects, or RAW files? 
 3 Is remote mobile access important? 
 How to choose
 Budget space for originals, exports, catalogs, and generated thumbnails.
 Prioritize mature photo software for family use; prioritize network speed and memory for large creator libraries.
 Keep an offline or cloud copy of original files.
 Avoid these mistakes
 Importing everything before a backup exists
 Underestimating RAW and video growth
 Assuming sync is the same as backup
 Frequently asked questions
 Can a home NAS completely replace Google Photos and Apple iCloud without subscription fees?
 A NAS can take over photo storage and sharing for some households, but it is not a like-for-like replacement for every cloud service. Check phone background uploads, remote access, family sharing, and the photo features you use. You still pay for hardware, electricity, maintenance, and an independent backup; a cloud copy may remain useful.
 Can photographers edit Lightroom RAW catalogs directly over a local network NAS?
 Lightroom Classic does not support keeping the active catalog on a network drive. Keep the catalog and previews on a local SSD; the original photos can live on the NAS. Faster networking can help import and export large files, but an SSD cache is not a prerequisite and will not remove every workflow bottleneck.
 Synology Photos vs. self-hosted Immich: Which one is better in 2026?
 Synology Photos fits owners who want photo management integrated into DSM. Immich fits owners comfortable managing a self-hosted application, its database, updates, and backups. Compare the features your family actually uses, then test a small library and a restore. Neither should hold the only copy of your originals.
 How much NAS storage is needed for a 10-year family photo and 4K video library?
 Measure the library you already have and last year’s growth. For example, 1TB today plus 300GB a year for ten years is 4TB before versions, exports, and free space, so a 4TB mirror would be too small. RAW and video workloads vary widely; size from your own files rather than an assumed household average.
 How do I share full-resolution photo albums securely with clients or extended family?
 NAS operating systems support password-protected public share links with optional expiration dates and download permissions. This allows family members or photography clients to view and download full-resolution RAW or JPEG files directly from your NAS without uploading them to third-party cloud hosts.

 How to Choose a NAS for Photography?
 Buying a NAS for photo storage is different from buying one for general home backup. Photographers care about three things above all else: enough bays for growing RAW libraries, fast enough networking to edit directly from the NAS, and software that doesn’t fight you when you have 50,000+ thumbnails. Here’s how to think through each decision.
 Bay Count and Storage Capacity
 Most photographers I work with regret buying a 2-bay unit within 18 months. A 4-bay is the minimum I recommend for working photographers because it gives you room for SHR or RAID 5 with a hot spare, plus room to grow without swapping drives. If you shoot weddings or events, expect your library to grow by 1-2TB per year. Landscape and portrait pros accumulate even faster when you count client galleries and RAW archives.
 A 6-bay unit like the Asustor AS6706T makes sense once your library crosses 40TB or you start adding video. The extra bays buy you time between drive upgrades and let you mix capacities more flexibly. For hobbyists with under 10TB, a 2-bay like the Synology DS225+ is still plenty if you commit to offloading older years to external cold storage.
 RAID Configurations Explained
 RAID is not a backup. It is a way to keep working when a single drive dies. For photographers, SHR (Synology Hybrid RAID) is the easiest starting point because it lets you mix drive sizes. RAID 5 gives you one drive of parity across 3+ disks, RAID 6 gives you two drives of parity across 4+ disks, and SHR-2 mirrors RAID 6’s two-disk redundancy with mixed sizes.
 My recommendation for most photographers is RAID 5 or SHR on a 4-bay, which gives you the capacity of N-1 drives. If you shoot weddings or run a studio where downtime is unacceptable, RAID 6 or SHR-2 is worth the capacity tradeoff for the extra redundancy. Whatever you choose, remember the rule: RAID protects you against drive failure, not against accidental deletion, file corruption, or ransomware. That is what backups are for.
 Network Speed: 1GbE vs 2.5GbE vs 10GbE
 The network port on your NAS is the bottleneck most photographers forget about. A 1GbE port tops out around 125 MB/s, which feels fast until you try to move a 500GB wedding folder. 2.5GbE bumps that to about 312 MB/s, which is plenty for most photo workflows and is the new sweet spot for home studios. 10GbE pushes 1,250 MB/s and lets you edit massive RAWs directly from the NAS with no perceptible lag.
 If your switch and computer both support 2.5GbE (most modern Macs and PCs do via USB adapters), the upgrade is one of the best price-to-performance moves you can make. 10GbE makes sense for studios with multiple editors or anyone working with 100MP+ medium format files. For everyone else, 2.5GbE is the right target.
 Software Ecosystem and Photo Apps
 The OS and apps matter more than the hardware for daily use. Synology Photos is the gold standard for face recognition and mobile integration, which is why Synology units remain popular for photographers. UGREEN’s AI Photo Album has caught up in 2026 and is arguably better for semantic scene search. Asustor’s ADM is solid but more generic, focusing on general NAS use rather than photography-specific workflows.
 If your existing workflow already depends on a specific photo app (like Lightroom catalog files), test it against your shortlist before buying. Some apps handle SMB shares better than others, and iSCSI behaves differently from NFS. For most photographers, SMB over 2.5GbE with the AI album features layered on top is the right combination.
 Backup Strategy: The 3-2-1 Rule
 A NAS is one copy. Photographers still need a true 3-2-1 backup: three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one off-site. In practice, that means your NAS as primary, an external USB drive as a local backup, and either a second NAS at a different location or a cloud backup like Backblaze B2 for the off-site copy.
 I run Hyper Backup on my Synology units to a remote NAS at my parents’ house and sync critical client galleries to Backblaze. The whole system costs about $7 per month and has already saved me once when a client accidentally deleted a gallery two days before delivery. Don’t trust your entire career to one box, no matter how good it is.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Do photographers need a NAS?
 Photographers benefit from a NAS once their library exceeds a single external drive or when multiple users need access. A NAS adds RAID protection so a single drive failure doesn’t lose your work, plus centralized access from any computer, phone, or tablet on your network. For working pros with client galleries, the automated backup and remote access features pay for themselves quickly.
 Is NAS better than DAS for photographers?
 NAS is better than DAS (Direct Attached Storage) when you need multi-user access, remote access, or automated RAID protection. DAS is faster per dollar and simpler for a single editor working at one desk. For most studios with more than one computer or anyone who wants to access files from a laptop on location, NAS provides flexibility that DAS cannot match.
 What is the best drive for storing photos?
 For NAS photo storage, use NAS-rated drives like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red Plus. These drives include vibration sensors and firmware tuned for 24/7 operation. Avoid desktop drives like WD Blue in a multi-bay NAS because they lack the rotational vibration compensation needed for reliable long-term use in an enclosure.
 What is the best NAS for photographers?
 The best NAS for photographers in 2026 is the Synology DS225+ for most users because of its Intel CPU, fast transfers, and best-in-class Synology Photos app. Power users with 10GbE networks should pick the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus for SSD-class speeds. Hobbyists on a budget get excellent value from the UGREEN DH4300 Plus with its 128TB capacity and AI Photo Album.
 What is the Synology controversy?
 The Synology controversy refers to recent policy changes around hard drive compatibility and some software restrictions introduced in 2024-2025, which frustrated long-time users. Synology’s hardware and software remain reliable for photography workflows, and DSM is still the most polished NAS operating system available. The controversy mainly affects users who want to use non-Synology-branded drives in newer enclosures.
 Final Verdict
 After 60 days of testing, the Synology DS225+ remains my top recommendation for most photographers looking for the best NAS drives for photographers in 2026. The Intel CPU, polished DSM software, and 3-year warranty hit the right balance of price, performance, and reliability. For studios with 10GbE networks, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is worth every penny. Hobbyists should grab the UGREEN DH4300 Plus and let the AI Photo Album handle the cataloging.
 Whatever you pick, finish the setup by configuring a real backup. A NAS is one copy, not a backup. Pair your new enclosure with an external USB drive and an off-site cloud sync, and you’ll never relive the 2 AM panic of a clicking external drive.  Why this matters
 Photography studios do not create files at a steady office pace. A wedding, school event, sports tournament or corporate conference can send several cards into the archive at once, followed by culling, editing, export and client delivery. Slow or scattered storage delays every stage.
 A NAS gives multiple computers controlled access to one central archive over the studio network. The right model also supports redundant drive layouts, snapshots and scheduled backups instead of leaving every photographer to manage separate portable drives.
 The NAS is only one part of a 2026 photography workflow. Camera cards or Beam camera-to-cloud FTP uploads handle ingest, the NAS holds the working archive, AI Culling removes duplicate and weak frames offline, and Foto Owl AI Gallery handles client delivery. A NAS should protect and organise source files; it should not become the client gallery. 
 The NAS protects the working archive while a gallery handles client-facing delivery. 
 What makes the best NAS for a photography studio
 Drive bays: Two bays suit a solo photographer using mirrored storage. Four or five bays give growing studios more capacity choices and better expansion paths.
 Network speed: Dual 2.5GbE ports or an optional 10GbE upgrade matter when several editors open RAW files, build previews or export finished galleries at the same time.
 RAID flexibility: RAID 1 suits two-drive systems. RAID 5 and hybrid RAID layouts make better use of four- and five-bay systems while retaining single-drive fault tolerance.
 NVMe support: M.2 NVMe slots can hold cache drives or fast storage volumes, depending on the NAS model and operating system.
 Snapshots and backup jobs: Snapshots help recover earlier file versions. Scheduled backup jobs create the separate copy that RAID does not provide.
 Expansion options: A NAS should accommodate the studio's next archive cycle without forcing a complete replacement.
 Software management: Clear permissions, storage alerts and remote administration reduce the chance of an editor changing the wrong folder or missing a failing drive.
 RAID is not the same as backup
 RAID keeps a compatible array operating when a covered drive failure occurs. It does not protect the studio when someone deletes a project folder, ransomware reaches the NAS, a power event damages the unit or the entire device is stolen.
 A practical 2026 setup follows the established 3-2-1 backup principle: keep three copies of important files, store them on two types of media and place one copy off-site. For a studio, that can mean a working NAS, a separate local backup and an off-site copy.
 Connect the NAS and network equipment to a compatible uninterruptible power supply. Configure automatic shutdown support where the NAS and UPS permit it. This is particularly important for Indian studios dealing with unstable power during long ingest or backup jobs.

 Best for: Studios with several photographers or editors accessing one active archive.
 Verdict: Buy. The Synology DiskStation DS1522+ is the stronger team option when five bays will be useful immediately.
 4. TerraMaster F4-423: best budget four-bay NAS
 The TerraMaster F4-423 provides four drive bays, dual 2.5GbE ports and two M.2 NVMe slots. Its hardware specification covers the core needs of a solo photographer who wants a four-bay array and faster-than-gigabit networking without prioritising the largest software catalogue.
 The decision comes down to administration. TerraMaster's operating system covers storage pools, user access and backup tasks, but photographers should confirm that every required backup destination and workflow application is supported before committing their archive.
 TerraMaster F4-423 pros: 
 Four internal bays allow RAID 5 and mirrored configurations.
 Dual 2.5GbE ports support faster local transfers on compatible networks.
 Two M.2 slots provide NVMe configuration options.
 The hardware suits photographers who expect their archive to grow.
 TerraMaster F4-423 cons: 
 The first-party application selection is smaller than Synology's catalogue.
 There is no internal drive-bay expansion path.
 Switching NAS ecosystems later requires migration planning.
 Best for: Solo photographers who want four bays and dual 2.5GbE while keeping the system focused on storage.
 Verdict: Buy. Choose the TerraMaster F4-423 when hardware value matters more than a broad application ecosystem.
 5. Synology DiskStation DS224+: best simple two-bay NAS
 The Synology DiskStation DS224+ is a two-bay system with dual 1GbE ports. Configure two matching drives as RAID 1 or Synology Hybrid RAID to maintain a mirrored copy when one drive fails.
 Its main strength is simplicity. A solo photographer gets the same core DiskStation Manager environment used by larger Synology units without planning a four- or five-drive array.
 Synology DiskStation DS224+ pros: 
 Two-bay design keeps RAID planning straightforward.
 Dual 1GbE ports support link aggregation on compatible networks.

 Compact dimensions suit a small studio workspace.
 Synology DiskStation DS224+ cons: 
 Storage cannot expand beyond two internal drive bays.
 Mirroring uses one drive's capacity for redundancy.
 1GbE networking limits direct multi-user editing compared with 2.5GbE or 10GbE systems.
 Best for: Solo photographers who need a central mirrored archive rather than a multi-editor storage server.
 Verdict: Hold if growth is likely; buy if two bays will cover the full retention plan. 
 How the NAS systems were ranked
 The ranking uses published manufacturer specifications for drive bays, network interfaces, NVMe support and expansion compatibility. It then weighs those features against photography-studio tasks: ingesting event files, creating previews, culling duplicates, sharing projects with editors and maintaining separate backups.
 Bay count and network options carry more weight than media-streaming features. A photography studio needs predictable file access and recoverable archives, not a long list of entertainment applications.
 Storage discipline also affects the result. Foto Owl AI Culling is an offline desktop application that rejects duplicate and weak frames, groups similar images, and ranks them by composition, exposure and blur before a human second pass. Following a faster photo-culling workflow prevents rejected frames from occupying long-term NAS and backup capacity.
 Which NAS storage system should you choose in 2026?
 Choose the Synology DiskStation DS923+ if you need one answer. It gives a growing studio four bays, NVMe options, a clear management system and a route to both additional bays and 10GbE networking.
 Choose the QNAP TS-464 when dual 2.5GbE and NVMe flexibility matter now. Choose the Synology DiskStation DS1522+ when several team members use the archive and five bays fit the storage plan. Pick the TerraMaster F4-423 for a storage-focused four-bay build, or the Synology DiskStation DS224+ for a simple two-drive mirror.
 Do not choose by enclosure alone. Budget for NAS-rated drives, compatible networking, an uninterruptible power supply and a separate backup destination. A fast NAS connected through a 1GbE switch will still operate at the slower network speed.
 Foto Owl belongs after storage and culling in this workflow. Its AI Gallery delivers selected photos and videos to clients with face recognition, while the NAS retains the studio's working files and source archive.
 FAQ
 What is the best NAS storage system for a photography studio in 2026?
 The Synology DiskStation DS923+ is the best overall NAS storage system for most photography studios in 2026. It combines four bays, NVMe support, expansion capability and an optional 10GbE upgrade.
 How many NAS drive bays does a wedding photography studio need?
 A solo wedding photographer can start with two mirrored bays, while a growing studio should choose four or five bays. More bays provide better capacity options and a longer expansion path.
 Is a NAS better than cloud storage for photographers?
 A NAS is better for fast local access to a working archive, while cloud storage provides off-site protection and remote access. Photography studios should use both rather than treating either one as the only copy.
 Can photographers edit RAW files directly from a NAS?
 Yes, photographers can edit RAW files directly from a NAS when the drives, network and computers support the required throughput. Dual 2.5GbE or 10GbE becomes more useful when several editors work concurrently.
 Does RAID count as a backup for wedding photos?
 No, RAID is not a complete backup because deletion, ransomware, theft or device damage can affect the entire array. Keep a separate local or off-site copy under a 3-2-1 backup plan.
 Should a photography NAS use SSDs or hard drives?
 Hard drives remain suitable for the main high-capacity archive, while supported NVMe SSDs can serve as cache or fast volumes. The correct configuration depends on the NAS model and the studio's actual bottleneck.
 Where does Foto Owl fit with NAS storage?
 Foto Owl AI Gallery handles client-facing photo and video delivery after files are culled and edited. The NAS remains the studio's local working archive, so the two systems perform separate jobs.
 Do photography studios need 10GbE networking?
 A solo photographer does not always need 10GbE, but multi-editor studios handling large RAW and video files can benefit from it. Every computer, cable and switch in the path must support the faster connection.
 One last thing
 Test recovery before the next paid event. Restore a complete project folder from the local backup and the off-site copy, then document the steps for the studio team. A backup that has never completed a restore is only an assumption.
 Foto Owl should receive the culled, edited files intended for clients; the NAS should retain the working archive according to the studio's retention policy. Keeping those roles separate makes the 2026 workflow easier to secure, maintain and scale.

 Buying Guide: How to Choose the Best NAS for Your Photography Workflow?
 Choosing the right NAS comes down to matching the hardware to how you actually shoot and edit. Here’s what to think about before you spend your money.
 Bay Count: Why 4+ Bays Matters for Photographers
 Every photographer I know has more photos than they thought they would. A 2-bay NAS feels roomy at first, but with RAID 1 mirroring, you get only half your raw capacity. After a few years of shooting, you’ll be hunting for external drives again.
 A 4-bay NAS gives you room to grow. In RAID 5, you lose only one drive’s worth of space to parity, so four 18TB drives give you 54TB of usable storage. That’s roughly 1.5 million RAW photos at 35MB each.
 For a multi-photographer studio or anyone shooting a lot of video, jump to 5 or 6 bays. The Synology DS1525+ in this list is the best example: 5 bays with room to expand to 300TB with an external unit.
 Network Speed: 1GbE vs 2.5GbE vs 10GbE
 The network port on your NAS matters more than most people think. A 1GbE connection maxes out at about 125 MB/s, which is slower than a spinning hard drive. You’ll feel it the moment you try to scrub a 4K timeline in Premiere.
 2.5GbE is the new sweet spot for photographers. It pushes 312 MB/s, which is faster than any single HDD and fast enough to edit most RAW files directly off the NAS. Most new NAS in this roundup include at least 2.5GbE, and the UGREEN DXP4800 GT has dual 10GbE for under $700.
 10GbE is only worth it if you’re editing 4K or 8K video or have multiple users hitting the NAS at once. For solo RAW photo work, 2.5GbE is enough.
 RAID Configuration: Protecting Your Photo Library
 RAID is not a backup. It protects you when a single drive fails, but it does not protect against fire, theft, ransomware, or accidental deletion. The 3-2-1 backup rule (3 copies, 2 different media types, 1 offsite) still applies.
 For photographers, RAID 5 or SHR (Synology Hybrid RAID) is the right starting point. You can lose one drive and still have all your photos. RAID 6 lets you lose two drives and is worth it for a 5+ bay unit holding your life’s work.
 For two-bay NAS, RAID 1 is your only safe option, and that limits capacity. It’s a key reason I recommend 4 bays as the minimum for serious photo storage.
 Drive Selection: NAS-Grade HDDs vs SSDs
 For bulk photo storage, NAS-grade hard drives like Seagate IronWolf or WD Red Pro are the right pick. They are built for 24/7 operation, include vibration sensors for multi-drive enclosures, and come with longer warranties (typically 3-5 years).
 SSDs are faster but cost roughly 5-8x more per terabyte. For a working photo library, the right answer is usually HDDs for bulk storage plus an SSD cache or a smaller SSD-only NAS (like the UGREEN DXP4800 GT with all-NVMe drives) for active editing projects.
 Photo Management Software Integration
 The best NAS for photographers is one that plays nicely with your existing workflow. If you use Lightroom or Capture One, almost any modern NAS will work, but the management software differs.
 Synology Photos is the most polished photo app, with excellent face recognition, mobile backup, and timeline browsing. UGREEN’s AI album is improving but not as refined. QNAP’s QuMagie is decent but feels a step behind both.
 For Lightroom specifically, you’ll want to map your NAS as a network drive and let Lightroom manage the catalog. SSD caching on the NAS (via NVMe) makes a real difference here.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best type of storage for a photographer’s work?
 For most photographers, the best storage strategy combines a 4-bay NAS with NAS-grade hard drives (Seagate IronWolf or WD Red Pro) in RAID 5 or RAID 6. This gives you large capacity, drive-failure protection, and network access from multiple computers. Add an SSD cache or an external backup for full 3-2-1 protection.
 What is the best NAS system for photographers?
 The best NAS for photographers is the UGREEN DXP4800 GT for raw speed and SD card imports, the Synology DS925+ for the best software ecosystem, and the Synology DS1525+ for studio-class multi-user editing. Beginners and home users should look at the UGREEN DH2300 or Synology DS223j.
 What is the best NAS app for storing photos?
 Synology Photos is the most polished photo app in the NAS world, with strong face recognition, timeline browsing, and mobile backup. UGREEN’s AI Album is a close second with local AI processing. QNAP’s QuMagie works but has fewer features.
 Is it better to store photos on SSD or HDD?
 HDDs are best for bulk photo storage because they cost roughly 5-8x less per terabyte than SSDs. SSDs are better for active editing projects, the OS drive, and caching. Most photographers run a hybrid setup: HDDs for the archive, SSDs for current work.
 Is a NAS worth it for photographers in 2026?
 Yes, a NAS is worth it for any photographer storing more than 1TB of photos, working on multiple computers, or worried about data loss. The upfront cost pays for itself in 2-3 years compared to cloud subscriptions, and you get faster network access plus full control of your files.
 Final Verdict: Which Best NAS for Photographers Should You Buy?
 After testing all 10 NAS units with my own photo libraries, the right answer depends on your workflow. For pure speed and the unique built-in SD card reader, the UGREEN DXP4800 GT is my editor’s choice and the best NAS for photographers who actually edit off the network. If you want Synology’s mature software and ECC memory for long-term archives, the Synology DS925+ is the safer pick. Studios and multi-photographer teams should invest in the Synology DS1525+ for its 5-bay flexibility and 10GbE readiness.
 For beginners and hobbyists, the UGREEN DH2300 is the easiest entry point, while the Synology DS223j gives you DSM access at the lowest price. And for anyone who wants the best mix of price, performance, and AI photo smarts, the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus remains the crowd favorite with 617 reviews to back it up.
 Whichever you pick, the most important step is actually setting up a backup. RAID protects against drive failure, but a proper 3-2-1 backup strategy protects against everything else. Start with the NAS, then add a second offsite copy (cloud or external drive stored elsewhere) before you trust it with your life’s work. If you’re curious how a NAS fits into the broader world of photography gear and outdoor adventures, check out our guides on the best NAS drives for photographers and best home NAS systems for more options. For those shooting wildlife, our 600mm lens guide pairs perfectly with a solid NAS backup strategy.
 Whatever you choose, the best NAS for photographers in 2026 is the one you’ll actually set up, populate with drives, and trust with your images. Stop scattering your work across external drives, and give your photos the safe home they deserve.

The 2.5GbE networking is the real upgrade over older 1GbE units – large RAW imports that used to take 12 minutes now finish in under 5 over a 2.5GbE switch.

 - The Bad
 Stock USB cable may be too long for 10Gbps transfers
 Power supply may struggle with 4 drives simultaneously
 Plastic case feels cheap
 The TERRAMASTER D4-320 is technically a direct-attached storage (DAS) enclosure, not a NAS, but we included it because photographers often use a 4-bay DAS as a fast local backup target that complements a smaller NAS. With USB 3.2 Gen 2 at 10Gbps, you get near-NAS speed for direct-attached workflows, and the tool-free drive bays are genuinely convenient for swapping drives in and out.
 For photographers who edit from a single workstation, the D4-320 is a smart play. Plug it into your editing computer, format the four drives in JBOD or as individual volumes, and you have a fast local pool for active projects. Transfer speeds over the 10Gbps USB connection hit around 800 MB/s with SSDs, and around 400 MB/s with spinning drives. That is fast enough to back up a 2TB shoot in under 90 minutes.
 Build quality is solid for the tier, and the tool-less drive caddies are the best feature – swapping a failed drive takes 10 seconds. The temperature-controlled fan is quiet in normal use. As a photographer’s local backup or shuttle drive, the D4-320 punches above its price tag.
 The caveats are real. This is not a NAS, so there is no RAID controller, no network sharing, and no app ecosystem. The included USB cable is longer than ideal for 10Gbps reliability – replace it with a shorter certified cable for best results. The plastic outer shell feels less premium than the metal enclosures higher in this roundup. And the power supply can struggle when 4 drives spin up simultaneously, which is a known issue TERRAMASTER has acknowledged in firmware updates.
 Who the TERRAMASTER D4-320 is good for
 This is the right pick for photographers who edit on a single workstation and want a fast, affordable local backup target. Wedding and event photographers shuttling data between locations will appreciate the tool-free drive caddies. Studios that already own a smaller NAS and want a high-capacity offline backup will find the D4-320 a strong value. It also works well as a media library for video editors who need fast direct-attached access.
 Who should skip the TERRAMASTER D4-320
 Skip this if you need network sharing, remote access, or any photo management app. A DAS is a complement to a NAS, not a replacement. If your workflow requires multiple editors accessing the same library, RAID protection against drive failure, or AI photo organization, jump back to one of the NAS units above. For photographers with multi-user studio workflows, the Synology DS925+ or QNAP TS-464 are the right picks.
 Check Latest Price on Amazon 
 Buying Guide: How to Choose the Best NAS for Your Photography
 Picking a NAS enclosure is not just about which one has the most drive bays. Photographers have specific needs around RAID protection, network speed, software features, and long-term reliability. Here is what actually matters when you are trusting a NAS with your image library.
 How many bays do photographers actually need
 Two bays are enough for most hobbyists and family libraries, especially if you are running RAID 1 (mirrored) for protection. Four bays make sense for working pros and studios because RAID 5 or RAID 6 gives you usable capacity plus tolerance for one or two drive failures. A good rule of thumb: if you shoot more than 50,000 images a year or your library is past 20TB, start with 4 bays. If you are still under 20TB and growing slowly, 2 bays will serve you well for years.
 Which RAID level protects photos best
 RAID is not a backup, but it does protect against a single drive failure. For 2-bay units, RAID 1 mirrors your data across both drives – you lose half the raw capacity but get full redundancy. For 4-bay units, RAID 5 gives you the capacity of 3 drives with tolerance for 1 failure, and RAID 6 gives you the capacity of 2 drives with tolerance for 2 failures. For photographers, RAID 5 is the common-sense minimum, and RAID 6 is worth the trade-off if your library is mission-critical. Always pair RAID with an offsite backup (cloud, second NAS, or tape) because RAID cannot save you from fire, flood, or accidental deletion.
 1GbE vs 2.5GbE vs 10GbE for photo workflows
 Network speed determines how fast you can move RAW files between your editing machine and the NAS. 1GbE tops out around 115 MB/s, which is fine for a single editor working on JPEGs but slow for multi-gigabyte RAW batches. 2.5GbE pushes that to about 280 MB/s and is the new sweet spot for home and small studio use – most modern motherboards support it, and 2.5GbE switches are affordable. 10GbE is overkill for most photographers but matters for studios with multiple editors or anyone working with high-resolution medium format files or 4K/8K video. The Synology DS925+ and QNAP TS-464 both support 2.5GbE natively, and the UGREEN DXP2800 adds dual 2.5GbE plus NVMe cache for the best of both worlds.
 Choosing the right hard drives for a photography NAS
 Do not put desktop drives in a NAS. NAS-rated drives like WD Red Plus, WD Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf, and Seagate IronWolf Pro are built for 24/7 operation, vibration tolerance, and longer warranties. For most photographers, 8TB to 16TB IronWolf or Red Plus drives hit the right balance of capacity, speed, and noise. Avoid shingled magnetic recording (SMR) drives in RAID arrays – they perform poorly during rebuilds. CMR (conventional magnetic recording) drives are the right choice.
 Synology Photos vs QuMagie vs UGOS Pro photo apps
 All three photo apps do the same core job: index your library, cluster faces, tag scenes, and let you share galleries. Synology Photos has the most mature feature set, the largest user community, and the best long-term support. QuMagie on QNAP is catching up fast and has a slightly more polished mobile app. UGOS Pro on UGREEN is newer but improving quickly, and the AI features work well. For photographers who value stability over novelty, Synology Photos is the safest bet. For those who want more features and do not mind a steeper learning curve, QuMagie and UGOS Pro are both worth considering.
 How to plan capacity for a growing photo library
 Estimate your annual growth in TB and multiply by 5. That gives you the capacity you should plan for over the next 5 years. A photographer shooting 30,000 RAW frames a year at 30MB per file generates roughly 900GB annually. Over 5 years, that is about 4.5TB of raw data, which fits comfortably in 2 bays with 8TB drives. A wedding shooter generating 3-5TB per year needs 4 bays with 16TB+ drives to keep growth headroom. Always leave at least 20% of your array free for snapshots, version history, and RAID parity overhead.
 How to budget realistically for a photography NAS
 The enclosure is the smaller piece of the budget. A 4-bay NAS enclosure runs a few hundred dollars, but filling it with 16TB IronWolf drives can easily add a thousand or more. Plan for the total cost of ownership: enclosure, drives, UPS battery backup, and a network switch if you do not already have one. Over 5 years, a properly built NAS is almost always cheaper than equivalent cloud storage subscriptions, especially once you account for the value of your time spent uploading and downloading files.
 What to know about the Synology drive compatibility changes
 Synology has tightened its drive compatibility policy in recent years, requiring certain NAS models to use Synology-branded drives for full warranty and feature support. This is a real change from the open third-party drive ecosystem photographers have relied on for over a decade. The DS223j, DS223, and DS925+ all support third-party drives for now, but the DS225+ has stricter requirements. If you are buying a Synology and want to use IronWolf or Red Plus drives, double-check the current compatibility list before you commit.
 For more on the wider NAS market, our guide to the best NAS systems for small business covers higher-capacity options, and our picks for NAS systems for Plex media streaming are worth a look if you also stream video. If you are still choosing a display to edit on, the best monitors for photographers guide is a good companion read.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Which NAS is best for photographer’s storage needs?
 For most photographers, the UGREEN DXP2800 and Synology DS225+ are the strongest picks. Hobbyists with libraries under 20TB will be well served by the Synology DS223j or UGREEN DH2300. Working pros and studios with 50,000+ images a year should consider the Synology DS925+ or QNAP TS-464 for 4-bay capacity, 2.5GbE networking, and faster AI indexing.
 What is the Synology controversy?
 In recent years Synology has tightened its drive compatibility policy, requiring certain newer NAS models to use Synology-branded drives for full warranty and feature support. This is a meaningful change from the open third-party drive ecosystem photographers relied on for over a decade, and it has generated active discussion on r/synology and r/datahoarder. Models like the DS223j, DS223, and DS925+ still support third-party drives, but the DS225+ has stricter requirements. Check the current Synology compatibility list before you commit to a drive purchase.
 Is a NAS good for storing photos?
 Yes, a NAS is one of the best options for storing photos. It gives you full data ownership, faster local access than cloud storage, unlimited capacity scaling, and features like AI photo recognition, automatic backup, and client sharing built in. Unlike cloud subscriptions, a NAS is a one-time hardware cost that pays for itself within a few years for active photographers. The main trade-off is that you are responsible for drive replacement, RAID maintenance, and offsite backup – but those are small tasks compared to monthly cloud fees.
 How many GB to store 10,000 photos?
 Storage requirements depend heavily on file format. Roughly: 50GB to 100GB for 10,000 smartphone JPEGs, 200GB to 400GB for 10,000 mirrorless or DSLR JPEGs, and 300GB to 600GB for 10,000 RAW files from a modern full-frame camera. Medium format RAW files push that to 1TB or more. Plan your NAS capacity for 5 years of growth, not just your current library – most photographers’ storage needs grow by 30% to 50% annually.
 What is the lifespan of a NAS drive?
 A NAS-rated hard drive typically lasts 3 to 5 years under 24/7 operation, though many run reliably for 7 years or more. Drive lifespan depends on workload, temperature, vibration, and power quality. NAS-rated drives like WD Red Plus, WD Red Pro, Seagate IronWolf, and Seagate IronWolf Pro are rated for higher workloads than desktop drives. Replace drives proactively around the 4-year mark, keep your NAS in a cool ventilated space, and always run it on a UPS battery backup to protect against power surges.
 Final Verdict: Which NAS Enclosure Should Photographers Buy
 After testing all eight units across a range of photography workflows, our top pick for the best NAS enclosure for photographers in 2026 is the UGREEN DXP2800 . It combines the strongest hardware in its tier (Intel N100, 8GB DDR5, 2.5GbE, dual NVMe), a polished software experience in UGOS Pro, and an attractive price that undercuts comparable Synology and QNAP units. For working photographers who shoot high volumes and need fast AI indexing, it is the most balanced enclosure we have tested this year.
 For photographers who prioritize software maturity and the deepest photo app ecosystem, the Synology DS225+ remains our runner-up. The Synology DSM experience and Synology Photos app are still the most refined in the industry, and the 3-year warranty plus easy migration from older Synology units make it a safe long-term investment. Studios and high-volume pros should look at the Synology DS925+ or QNAP TS-464 for 4-bay capacity and 2.5GbE networking.
 Whatever NAS you choose, pair it with NAS-rated CMR drives, a UPS battery backup, and an offsite backup plan. The combination of RAID protection, offsite redundancy, and the convenience of having your entire image library accessible from any device is what makes a NAS the right call for serious photographers. Once you live with one for a few months, going back to a stack of external drives or a cloud subscription feels like a step backward.

Best NAS for Photographers and Post Production – NAS Compares 
 Why use a NAS for your Photography and Video Editing
 NAS has fast become the go-to storage medium for both home and working professionals in 2018. Photo and video editors the world over are turning to network attached storage to bolster and improve their workflow. Gone are the days when a photo and video editors content would be moved around on a USB drive from place to place. Now almost every part of the data workflow and editing chain has changed for users from original capture through to post-production and so distribution can all be conducted safely and securely on a single NAS storage device. However, buying your first NAS can be a difficult and confusing process, investing in the wrong solution can end up costing you serious money. So today I want to discuss the right points to consider when buying your first photo and video storage NAS. I want to focus on those whose businesses revolve around the creation and distribution of their original content – whether you are a content creator for YouTube and other video on demand (VoD) services or a professional photographer that needs secure RAID storage with the flexibility that really only a NAS can provide. 
 Choosing the right NAS for your photo and video editing in pre and post production means that you want to do most of the work in one place. A normal scenario and workflow for post-production go as follows. First, your created Media that has been recorded or captured by a camera needs to be uploaded to your storage device either via USB connection or SD card slot. Of course, if you are fortunate enough to own a capture device that is network supported, you will be able to upload directly to the NAS via your network or the internet.
 It is worth mentioning now that the perfect NAS for photo and video editing is one that is both fast and arrives with a solid RAID protection. RAID stands for redundant array of independent disks. In real terms, this means that in the event of media hardware failure your data can be both protected and retrieved. The more data you create, the more important RAID will become as you will use more and more hard drives or SSD to store this media. So those that want a long-term RAID-enabled NAS solution should look towards 4 Bay NAS devices and larger as well as RAID configurations such as RAID 5 and RAID 6 for those who want an extra layer of hardware protection.
 Now your data is stored on the NAS, and hopefully RAID protected, we can talk about editing the files on the NAS live. If you intend to edit files that live directly on a NAS server device it is worth mentioning that larger files will require a faster connection than typically most homes and office have by default. Most typical network setups run at one gigabit per second ethernet (1Gbe). This is more than enough for backing up and streaming content two devices throughout the network, but if you want to edit large and complex files on your connected Mac or Windows machine that are stored on the NAS (so the file is not held on your local machine) you will need something much faster.
 Most NAS devices are NLE Compatible ( non-linear editing) and therefore the device and the data will be visible for editing on your desired software. Post Production software that use NLE use copies of the files over the network/externally so original files are untouched on the NAS, but still also using non-local drives for source and production media (the NAS).  It is also worth mentioning that you will need to ensure that the NAS you use is  Compatible with popular NLE such as Adobe Premiere, Apple Final Cut Pro X, Avid Media Composer…and more for 4K video editing 
 If you are editing HD 4K and raw photography then 1Gbe speed will be insufficient for editing and will lead to network lag and editing programs freezing as they are unable to edit the digital assets on the NAS at a fast enough speed. If you are considering editing files on a NAS then you will need to consider faster NAS Solutions, such as thunderbolt connected NAS from QNAP and 10-gigabit ethernet NAS devices. These are available from many of the top tier NAS brands and arrive in 10Gbe over SFP+ (fiber) or 10GBASE-T (RJ45 based and the same connection as your regular network devices).
 Of the two options, SFP+ is the most expensive of the two by far but can maintain speeds for a great deal further. 10GBASE-T is very similar to existing cables, can be mixed with your 1Gbe devices and is lower both in overall cost and if you want to upgrade gradually. If you want to upgrade to 10Gbe you will need to take into account that in order to fully take advantage of this speed you will need a 10GBe enabled Switch and upgrading each applicable device to 10GBe with a 10GBe PCIe card or a Thunderbolt-to-ethernet adapter for 10G.
 Recommended Network Switches for NAS in 2018 
 See more 
 Lastly, if you intend to use some of the mass storage for scraped data and for storing temporary files for editing, then you would be recommended to install at least one SSD drive into the NAS for this purpose and creating a pool of SSD cache. This is incredibly straightforward and something that the likes of Synology and QNAP have been making more and more available within their respective user interfaces in 2018.
 https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bEwSw9bZWDc
 Once your files have been edited and you have closed editing on the file, creating your finished product, the next important part of the NAS device becomes clear – Distribution. The versatility of a NAS device to distribute files on your internal network or the internet cannot be overstated. With two-step verification and multi-layered permission-based access that can be granted or removed at a moments notice, many photographers and videographers will use a NAS to distributional products.
 Likewise thanks to snapshot backups and version based storage backups, you are able to keep many versions of the same file and revert back to an earlier version in the event this is required. As well as permissions and control of access for your intended viewers, the contents of a NAS is also heavily encrypted via a 256 bit algorithm. Lastly due to increased administration control for up to 25 users and unlimited user account creation for those with less responsibility or Access permissions, you are able to create a secure network for your files and how they are distributed internally and externally.
 It is certainly worth mentioning that if you create video footage that you wish to stream to users on a paid for video on demand platform, then a NAS will very quickly pay for itself in terms of hosting video streaming services from your own home or small office network
 What are the key things to consider in a Perfect Post Production NAS
 Below is a basic workflow of production and where a NAS lives in that chain, as well as what you need to consider.
 Normal NAS Production Workflow: 
 You Create your Media. A Vlogger for YouTube, a Wedding Photographer on site, a Broadcaster preparing footage.
 PHOTO/VIDEO CREATED ON CAMERA/CAPTURE DEVICE 
 If your recording device is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as the NAS or the internet, this will enable footage to be directly sent to the NAS after capture. If you are concerned about file size, then you can use a NAS with an SD Card slot or one of the MANY USB Card Readers that are compatible with Synology or QNAP NAS.
 UPLOADED TO NAS OVER INTERNET/NETWORK/USB LOCALLY 
 Once the files are on the NAS system, you have several Options. You can assign them to their own folder, create a duplicate automatically for editing (so the original stock footage is safe), put them in a shared (by protected) folder, create an ISCSI volume so the media is visible as an available drive to supported client software, create a network drive that can be seen and added by client devices and more. Most of these things can be set up for the first time and automatic afterwards.
 PREPARE TO EDIT FILES ON THE NAS 
 How the files are edited will depend on factors like:
 Network Speed  – If you are going to edit over the network, then you will either be using 1Gbe (the default), 10Gbe (upgrade) or 40GBe (much more expensive and only supported by a handful of NAS devices currently)
 Thunderbolt NAS editing – If you buy a NAS from QNAP or Synology that supports Thunderbolt, then it is worth remembering that the CPU inside should be at least an Intel Celeron for HD file editing and an i3, i5 or i7 for larger RAW or 4K editing. Also, the protocol for editing over a Thunderbolt NAS is known as ‘Thunderbolt-over-IP’ and not quite as straightforward as regular plug-n-play. It is pretty straightforward but just needs a few extra minutes at first setup. Be sure to check your intended editing software supports Thunderbolt over IP.
 SEND/SHARE/DISTRIBUTE 
 Once the completed project is on the NAS, there are numerous ways to share and distribute your media. You can create tailored shared volumes and folders that can be accessed over the internet by users to whom you send the valid web link. These can be accessed with a simple password or full account setup and access if you want more information and security. You can create hundreds of shares and each can be controlled and monitored (with security and restrictions as you see fit). This method is especially useful to photography professionals such as wedding photographers who want to create folders of completed images for clients that they can view but not save, as well as be retrieved for their websites behind a login/paywall. Alternatively, if you want to distribute your work to colleagues, you can create user groups for NAS access where they have limited control and cannot alter/delete/move any file/folder, but have access to the files you designate to their user group/profile. These can be created one by one or by uploading an existing user CSV to the NAS.
 ARCHIVE IN NAS FOLDERS TO TO ANOTHER NAS OVER NETWORK 
 Once your campaign is complete, then you need to think about long-term storage and archiving. This can be handled by the NAS in a number of ways. You can set up a separate RAID volume inside the NAS that will handle the long-term/cold storage of old projects (which can be manually passed over or automatically setup over time). Alternatively, you can set up a separate NAS in your network or off-site over the internet and via methods like cloud-sync, RSync and Real Time Remote Replication (RTRR) and have these files backed up offsite, away from your daily storage device. Finally most NAS server devices feature USB 3.1 or USB 3.1 Gen 2, which means that files can be automatically backed up to a USB device that is connected to the NAS (or actioned manually if you like with a one-touch-copy button) so then you have a copy of all your data (or just a few select folders, whichever you prefer) which can be taken away home or storage somewhere secure.
 Now you are ready for your next big project!
